Frequently Asked Questions

Dubai Real Estate FAQs: Off-Plan, Costs, Visas and Buyer Protection

Clear answers on buying costs, off-plan payments, visas and buyer protection in Dubai.

HomeFAQs

Buying in Dubai is straightforward when you know the full cost, the payment process, and your protections. These answers cover off-plan and ready property for local and overseas buyers.

Please read first: This page is general information only. It is not legal, tax, financial, mortgage, investment or immigration advice. It is not an offer to sell, buy or rent any property, and it is not a guarantee of any outcome. Rules, fees and visa requirements can change. Always confirm figures, eligibility and contract terms with the Dubai Land Department (DLD), RERA, your bank, or a licensed professional before you make a payment or sign anything.

Last updated: November 2026

1. What additional costs are generally involved when buying off-plan in Dubai?

Costs can vary by project and by developer. As a general guide, buyers often budget for:

  • DLD registration fee: Generally 4% of the purchase price, usually paid via Oqood registration. This is generally the main government registration fee, not an additional fee on top of Oqood.
  • Oqood and admin fees: Often around AED 4,020 for DLD admin, plus small knowledge and innovation fees. These amounts may change.
  • Developer admin fee: Varies by developer and project. Some developers may waive it as part of a launch offer. Ask for it in writing before booking.

Your instalments after booking are generally paid according to the payment plan in your Sales and Purchase Agreement (SPA). Always check your own SPA.

2. What additional costs are generally involved when buying a ready or secondary property in Dubai?

For a completed resale property, buyers often budget for:

  • DLD transfer fee: Generally 4% of the purchase price.
  • Trustee office fee: Often AED 2,000 plus VAT for properties below AED 500,000, and AED 4,000 plus VAT for properties at AED 500,000 and above. These amounts may change.
  • Title deed issuance: Often around AED 580.
  • Agency commission: Often around 2% of the price plus 5% VAT on a secondary purchase. The exact commission should be agreed in writing before transfer.
  • Developer NOC fee: Varies by developer and community. Your agent can help you confirm the current amount before transfer.
  • Mortgage costs, if financed: Mortgage registration is generally 0.25% of the loan amount plus AED 290 admin, plus bank valuation and processing fees, subject to the bank.

As a general guide only, many cash buyers budget around 7% to 8% on top of the price for a resale purchase. Your actual total will depend on your property, your financing and your contract.

3. Is it possible to sell an off-plan property before completion?

In many cases, yes, but it depends on your SPA and the developer. Many developers may allow resale once you have paid around 30% to 40% of the price and settled the DLD fee. You may also need a developer No Objection Certificate (NOC) and you may need to pay an assignment or NOC fee. The threshold, fee and process can vary by developer and project. If a possible early exit matters to you, confirm these terms in your SPA before you buy.

4. What generally happens if the developer delays the project or the project is cancelled?

Delays are generally handled under your SPA. Many SPAs include a grace period for handover. Check the exact clause in your own SPA.

For registered off-plan projects, buyer payments are generally required to go into a project-specific escrow account supervised under the RERA framework. Funds are generally intended to be released to the developer only against certified construction progress.

If RERA cancels a project by a final decision, refunds are generally handled through the escrow process. The timing, process and amount can vary and may depend on the official cancellation process and what is available in escrow. No specific refund amount or timeline is guaranteed.

5. What generally happens to Dubai property if the owner passes away? Who may inherit it?

This can depend on faith, family circumstances, and whether a valid will is registered. It can be complex. Independent legal advice is recommended.

For Muslim owners, Sharia succession rules may generally apply.

For non-Muslim owners, Federal Decree-Law No. 41 of 2022 may allow you to leave your UAE assets to persons you choose in a will. Without a will, the estate may generally be divided with half to the surviving spouse and half split equally among the children, subject to the applicable law.

Non-Muslim owners often register a will with the DIFC Wills Service or a notarised will at Dubai Courts. If you own property in Dubai, consider speaking to a licensed wills and succession lawyer about your family situation.

6. What generally happens if property prices fall after I buy off-plan?

In general, the SPA remains binding subject to its terms. A fall in market value does not automatically cancel the contract or reduce the balance you agreed to pay.

Plan for this risk before booking. If you are using a mortgage, note that the bank may value the property at handover, and a lower valuation may create a gap you need to cover in cash. Speak to your bank about this risk.

7. How are off-plan payments generally handled? Are they protected?

Under Dubai Law No. 8 of 2007, registered off-plan projects are generally required to have a dedicated escrow account with an approved UAE bank.

Your payments are generally required to go into that project escrow account, not into an agent personal account or a general developer account. The account is generally named in your SPA. Before you pay, verify the escrow account details in your SPA and on the DLD project record, and always keep your payment receipts.

Escrow is designed to reduce risk. It does not remove all investment risk. Always check the developer track record and project status, and consider independent advice.

8. Is it generally possible to buy a Dubai property without visiting Dubai?

In many cases, yes. Many overseas buyers complete much of the off-plan process remotely.

For off-plan, you may be able to reserve, sign the SPA electronically, and complete Oqood registration with a copy of your passport, subject to developer and KYC requirements. For a ready or resale property, a representative may be able to sign at the trustee office under a Power of Attorney (POA).

A POA signed abroad generally needs to be notarised, legalised and attested for use in the UAE, so allow time for this. You may still need to visit Dubai later for visa biometrics, or for opening a UAE bank account or mortgage, depending on your case.

9. What generally happens if I miss an off-plan instalment?

Do not ignore it. Contact your developer and your agent as soon as possible.

The process generally involves:

  • Step 1: The developer notifies the Dubai Land Department (DLD) of the default.
  • Step 2: DLD may serve an official 30-day notice to settle the amount or reach a settlement.
  • Step 3: If you do not pay or settle within that period, the developer may seek to cancel the agreement under the statutory process.

If the contract is cancelled, the developer may seek to retain a portion based on construction progress, generally up to 25% if construction is below 60% and up to 40% if construction is between 60% and 80%. Above 80%, the developer may instead seek the balance, ask DLD to auction the unit, or terminate under the same cap, subject to the law and your SPA. Any balance, if payable, is generally handled under that process.

Your SPA may also include late payment penalties. Acting early, for example by seeking a settlement or a possible resale before termination, is often better than waiting. Seek independent advice if you are in this situation.

10. Is it possible to get a UAE visa or Golden Visa by buying property in Dubai?

It may be possible, subject to approval and current authority requirements. A purchase does not automatically give you a visa.

10-Year Golden Visa: You may be eligible if you own property worth AED 2 million or more. This may be one property or a portfolio in your name. Mortgaged property may qualify with a bank letter or NOC confirming at least AED 2 million has been paid, subject to current requirements.

2-Year Property Investor Visa: If you are the sole owner of a completed property, there may currently be no minimum property value requirement. If the property is jointly owned, each investor may need to hold a share worth at least AED 400,000 to qualify, subject to current requirements.

Visas are not guaranteed with purchase. You must still meet medical, insurance, documentation and authority approval requirements. Confirm your eligibility before booking if a visa is a main reason for buying.

11. What ongoing costs should I generally expect after handover?
  • Service charges: Generally charged per sq. ft. per year and can vary by building and community. They may cover maintenance, security, common areas, and community facilities. Ask for the current service charge for your exact unit before booking.
  • Utility connection: DEWA deposit and connection fees at handover may apply.
  • Property management: If you plan to rent it out, management fees may apply if you use a property manager.

Ask for the service charge, expected handover fees and first-year running costs in writing before you commit.

12. Is it generally possible for a non-resident to get a mortgage in Dubai?

In many cases, yes, but terms are often stricter than for residents and approval is not guaranteed. Banks generally require proof of income, bank statements, proof of address, and a good credit history. Loan-to-value ratios for non-residents are often lower, and interest rates and fees can vary by bank and applicant. If you need finance, consider getting a pre-approval or at least a bank eligibility check before you reserve, especially for off-plan purchases where instalments are time-bound.

13. How can I generally verify a developer and project before I pay?

Before booking, consider checking:

  • Whether the project is registered with DLD and has an active escrow account.
  • Whether the developer name, project name and escrow account in your SPA match the DLD record.
  • The developer track record for delivery, quality and handover.
  • The payment plan, handover date, grace period and resale or NOC terms in the SPA.

A genuine agent should be willing to share the SPA, project registration details and escrow information before asking for payment. Do not rely only on marketing material.
